    AI Overview
    You can get an automatic six-month extension to file your federal income tax return, moving the deadline from April 15 to October 15, by filing Form 4868 by the April 15 deadline. This extension is only for submitting paperwork; any taxes owed must still be paid by April 15 to avoid penalties. 
    How to File a Tax Extension 
    • IRS Free File: Use free tax software to electronically file Form 4868, regardless of your income.
    • Pay Electronically: Make a payment via IRS Direct Pay, debit/credit card, or Digital Wallet and select "Extension" as the payment type. You will receive a confirmation number and do not need to file Form 4868.
    • Mail Form 4868: Complete Form 4868 and mail it to the IRS postmarked by April 15. 
    Important Considerations 
    • Not an Extension to Pay: The extension only gives you more time to submit your return. You must estimate and pay your tax liability by April 15 to avoid interest and late payment penalties.
    • Failure-to-File Penalty: Filing an extension prevents the 5% penalty (of unpaid taxes) per month for not filing, which can reach up to 25%.
    • Disaster Relief: Taxpayers in specific disaster areas may be granted longer extensions automatically.
    • Military/Foreign: Individuals stationed outside the U.S. or in combat zones may have specific, longer deadlines.

    Can I get another tax extension after October 15?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    No, you generally cannot file a second automatic tax extension after October 15. The IRS only allows one automatic six-month extension, bringing the final filing deadline to October 15 for most individuals. Missing this date often results in failure-to-file penalties, though special circumstances like disasters or being outside the US can sometimes allow extra time. 
    What to Know After October 15 
    • No Further Auto-Extension: The IRS typically does not offer a second extension beyond October 15 for personal tax returns.
    • Penalties for Late Filing: The failure-to-file penalty is usually 5% of the unpaid taxes for each month the return is late, up to 25%.
    • Exceptions:
      If you are a U.S. citizen living abroad or were impacted by a natural disaster, you may qualify for more time.
    • What to Do Now: Even if you cannot pay what you owe, file your return immediately to stop the failure-to-file penalty from increasing.
    • Payment Plans: If you owe money, you can request an additional 60–120 days to pay through an Online Payment Agreement or by calling the IRS. 
    If you are dealing with special circumstances, such as being in a combat zone or in a disaster area, you should check for special instructions that may extend the deadline automatically.

      How to file for a tax extension

      While you will get more time to file your return, an extension does not grant you more time to pay your taxes. To avoid possible penalties, you should estimate and pay your federal taxes by the due date.

      Learn the ways to request an extension:
      • Online using IRS Free File
      • When you pay your estimated tax bill
      • Using IRS Form 4868
      How to pay taxes in installments

      If you feel that you may not be able to pay your tax bill in full by the due date, you may be eligible to pay in installments. Learn more about the IRS' payment plans and what additional costs and fees you may have to pay.
